title: The Draftsman Who Invented Modern Copyright
event_summary: In January 1710, a little-known Scottish bookseller and political operative named John Baskett lobbied alongside a coalition of London stationers to push through the Statute of Anne — but its true architect was largely Daniel Defoe, who years earlier had published pamphlets arguing that authors, not printers, owned their words. The statute, enacted April 10, 1710, became the world's first law to vest copyright in authors rather than in royal-chartered printing guilds, granting them a fixed 14-year term of exclusive rights. This single piece of legislation demolished the centuries-old assumption that ideas belonged to whoever physically controlled the press.
why_forgotten: The Statute of Anne is overshadowed by Defoe's later fame as the novelist who wrote Robinson Crusoe, and legal historians long treated copyright as an arcane subset of commercial regulation rather than a transformative philosophical shift. The London Stationers' Company, which lost its monopoly, had little interest in celebrating the law, and the statute's quiet passage amid the drama of Queen Anne's wars further buried it from popular memory.
why_it_matters: Every modern copyright law on Earth — from Hollywood licensing to digital streaming royalties to open-source software — descends directly from the principles codified in this statute. By establishing that creators have time-limited ownership of their work, it created the entire economic architecture of the modern creative industries, and the debates it sparked about access versus ownership are the exact controversies driving today's battles over AI training data, fair use, and digital piracy.
